title: A Clean Slate for Offline Reinforcement Learning

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The abstract claims 'average training speedups of 131.5× and 74.8× against OfflineRL-Kit [16] and CORL [17]'. However, the only speedup data presented are Figure 5 (showing per‑algorithm speedups between 4× and 16×) and Table 2 (training times that give per‑algorithm speedups roughly 6–20× against OfflineRL‑Kit and 1–18× against CORL). The claimed averages of 131.5× and 74.8× are an order of magnitude larger than any supported value and are contradicted by the paper's own evidence.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 5.2 (paragraph describing Figure 7) and subsequent sentence
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text states: 'Figure 7 shows how MoBRAC outperforms other model‑based methods for all datasets, except for MOPO in maze2d‑large‑v1.' Immediately after it says: 'Under a transparent evaluation budget, we find that MoBRAC outperforms the other model‑based methods in 6 out of 9 datasets and is tied with MOPO for 3 others.' The first claim implies outperformance on 8 of 9 datasets; the second says 6 outperforms and 3 ties. These two statements about the same experimental results are contradictory and cannot both be true.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix G, Table 3 and the claim of reproduction
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper states in Appendix G that the reimplementations match the performance of prior implementations (citing [17]), yet the EDAC results in Table 3 are clearly broken: HalfCheetah‑expert 2.3±0.0, Hopper‑expert 4.9±0.2, Walker2d‑expert 79.0±45.3. These values are far below the expected performance of EDAC (typically >100 on locomotion expert tasks) and do not match the published results the authors claim to reproduce. This indicates either a flawed implementation or misreported numbers, undermining the claimed correctness of the reimplementations.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix I.1, Equation (7) and accompanying text
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The unified critic diversity loss is defined as the sum of inner products of critic gradients with respect to the action: ⟨∇_{a_t} q_i(s_t, a_t), ∇_{a_t} q_j(s_t, a_t)⟩. The original EDAC algorithm uses the cosine similarity (normalized dot product) to measure diversity, not the raw dot product. Using the unnormalized dot product changes the behavior of the penalty and does not faithfully represent the method being unified. This misrepresents a core component of EDAC within the proposed unified framework.
